question: What are the borders of Israel?
summary: The Bible draws the borders of the Promised Land at least three different ways. Genesis 15:18 and Exodus 23:31 stretch from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; Numbers 34 carves out a much smaller box basically the size of Canaan; and Ezekiel 47 draws a third map with Damascus on the northern edge and the Dead Sea region to the south. These aren't the same territory.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read the differing maps as one idealized grant that Israel never fully occupied, not three rival territories.

discrepancy.connective: Steven DiMattei presses the opposite case, arguing the passages preserve variant scribal traditions from different periods that genuinely disagree on where the borders run.

skeptic.name: Steven DiMattei
skeptic.attribution: Dr. Steven DiMattei, Contradictions in the Bible, #343 “Variant Traditions on the Borders of the Promised Land”

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Genesis 15:18
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this exact tension: he notes the Genesis grant is far wider than the narrower bounds 'fixed much narrower, Num 34:2, Num 34:3,' and harmonizes them by appeal to maximal extent under David and Solomon plus Israel's own forfeiture of the fuller territory.

link.note: No allowlisted page (gotquestions.org / carm.org / defendinginerrancy.com) was found that engages this specific three-map tension (Gen/Exod vs Num 34 vs Ezek 47); the closest allowlisted pages treat only the Joshua 1:4 / Joshua 13 occupation question, so the optional link is omitted per the reality bar.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Here, God reviewed the plan and identified the boundaries of the Promised Land in an idealized form (cp. Josh 13–19; Ezek 47–48). Old Testament Israel did not possess the exact extent of the territory described here (though it came close in the days of David and Solomon; e.g., 2 Sam 24:1-9), but these borders describe the region of Canaan as generally defined by Egyptian texts dating 1500–1200 BC (the period of the Hebrew invasion).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly engages why the maps differ: frames Numbers 34 (and by cross-reference Ezek 47) as an idealized boundary that Israel never fully occupied, with David/Solomon as the near-realization of the larger Genesis/Exodus extent — the core harmonization of the three-map tension. Capped to a single strongest excerpt to keep parity with the single named-skeptic discrepancy pole (discrepancy_first).
excerpts.source_note_text: 34:1-29 Chapter 34 gives the borders of the land of Canaan, which Israel was to settle according to the guidelines in 26:52-56. Ever since the call of Abraham (Gen 12:1-7), the Promised Land of Canaan had stood at the heart of the Old Testament story. Though an entire generation of Hebrews died in the wilderness because they refused to believe the report of the faithful spies (Num 13), God had reaffirmed his promise of land (33:53). Here, God reviewed the plan and identified the boundaries of the Promised Land in an idealized form (cp. Josh 13–19; Ezek 47–48). Old Testament Israel did not possess the exact extent of the territory described here (though it came close in the days of David and Solomon; e.g., 2 Sam 24:1-9), but these borders describe the region of Canaan as generally defined by Egyptian texts dating 1500–1200 BC (the period of the Hebrew invasion). The region actually occupied by Israel changed from time to time.
